If the knights of ren decided to turn against the first order as a third party, would it be in character, and a clever move, for Hux to disguise a thermal detonator as a holocron, and putting it on

message.content: Assuming “putting it on” means placing the disguised holocron on a table, pedestal, or negotiation surface, the idea is in character for Hux only if it is a proud, theatrical trap rather than a subtle espionage trick. Hux is not the kind of character who would quietly become a master spy or patiently build an elaborate covert operation. He is insecure, status-obsessed, and easily offended by anyone who outshines him. If the Knights of Ren are acting as a third party and the First Order is losing control of Kylo, Hux might very well want to stage a humiliating demonstration of power. A fake holocron could fit his instincts if it is presented as a trophy, a piece of Jedi history, or a bargaining chip. He would not necessarily disguise the detonator himself with Jedi knowledge; more likely, First Order technicians would create a convincing shell, and Hux would use it because it lets him appear knowledgeable, dangerous, and superior to the Ren faction. The move is clever because it weaponizes the First Order’s fear of Jedi relics and the Knights of Ren’s tendency to treat symbols as leverage. A thermal detonator shaped like a holocron is a good asymmetrical trap because it turns a sacred or valuable-looking object into a threat. The Knights of Ren are not Jedi, but they are still connected to the Jedi world, and a holocron would likely be something they would want to inspect, claim, or use as proof of power. If Hux puts it on the table as a gesture of confidence, the trap works not because the detonator is technically brilliant, but because it exploits expectation. The audience, the Ren, and possibly Kylo would all see the holocron and read meaning into it. That makes the object more dangerous than a plain bomb. It is a symbol with a fuse. It becomes dramatically plausible when Hux is not simply hiding a bomb but staging a display that exposes his insecurity, ambition, and hatred of Kylo’s independent power. If the holocron is placed on display, Hux is doing more than setting a trap; he is trying to control the room. He wants to be seen as the one who captured a Jedi artifact, the one who can use it, the one who is not intimidated by the Knights of Ren. That is very Hux. He is constantly performing authority he does not fully possess. If the Ren turn against the First Order, Hux would likely see that as a personal challenge, not just a military one. Placing the fake holocron on the table or pedestal would be his way of saying, “I know what these things are, and I can use them against you,” even if his confidence is fragile. The trap works best if it is also a bluff. The plan risks becoming out of character if Hux has to understand Jedi lore better than the film gives him, or if the trap works too neatly without forcing a character choice. Hux should not be written as though he suddenly understands how holocrons function, what they contain, or how a Force-sensitive would interact with them. He may know that the First Order fears Jedi relics, but he would not know the details. If he personally crafts the disguise, that would strain credibility. If he obtains a real holocron shell, a confiscated replica, or a military fabrication, that is much more believable. Also, the cleverness should not come from Hux being smarter than everyone else; it should come from the fact that the Ren, Kylo, Rey, and even the audience all make assumptions about what the object means. The trap is best when it creates a moment of choice: does the Ren take it? Does Kylo warn Hux? Does Rey realize it is fake before it detonates? If the detonation is merely a surprise explosion, it becomes less character-driven and more like a simple MacGuffin. So yes: Hux could disguise a thermal detonator as a holocron and place it on display as a clever move, provided the scene is about status, fear, and the failure of pride rather than Hux becoming a covert genius. The strongest version of the idea is not “Hux secretly booby-traps a holocron,” but “Hux publicly displays a fake holocron to prove he is not afraid of the Ren or the Jedi legacy, and his own arrogance makes the object lethal.” If the Knights of Ren are a third party, Hux would be trying to assert First Order dominance while secretly resenting Kylo’s independence. A disguised detonator shaped like a holocron fits that perfectly if it is played as a bluff, a status symbol, and a trap born of insecurity. It is in character when it reveals Hux’s flaw: he would rather be feared and seen in control than admit he is losing influence.
